paragraphs: Long ago, in my grandmother’s time, the Carland was all bogs: great pools of black water, creeping trickles of green water, and squelching mud that squirted when you stepped on it.
Well, Granny used to say that, long before her time, the Moon herself had once been dead and buried in the marshes. I’ll tell you all about it, just as Granny told me.
The Moon up there shone and shone, just as she does now. When she shone, she lit the bog pools so that people could walk about almost as safely as in daylight.
But when she did not shine, out came the Things that lived in the darkness and went about seeking to do evil and harm. Goblins and Crawling Horrors all came out when the Moon did not shine.

Well, the Moon heard about this. Being kind and good—as she surely is, shining for us at night instead of taking her natural rest—she was deeply troubled. “I’ll see for myself, I will,” she said. “Perhaps it isn’t as bad as people say.”

Sure enough, at the end of the month she stepped down, wrapped in a black cloak, with a black hood over her shining yellow hair. She went straight to the edge of the bog and looked around. Water here, water there; waving clumps of grass, trembling mud, and great black tree stumps, twisted and bent. Everything ahead was dark—dark except for the stars glimmering in the pools and the light from her own white feet, slipping out beneath her black cloak.

The Moon pulled her cloak tighter around herself and trembled. But she would not go back without seeing everything there was to see. On she went, stepping as lightly as a summer wind from tuft to tuft between the greedy, gurgling water holes. Just as she neared a large black pool, her foot slipped, and she almost fell in. She caught a nearby stump with both hands to steady herself. But the moment she touched it, it wound around her wrists like a pair of handcuffs and gripped her so tightly that she could not move. She pulled and twisted and fought, but it was no use. She was trapped, and trapped she had to stay.

As she stood trembling in the dark, wondering whether help would come, she heard something calling in the distance—calling, calling, then fading into a sob, until the marshes were full of that pitiful crying. Then she heard footsteps floundering along, squelching in the mud and slipping on the tufts. Through the darkness she saw a white face with wide, frightened eyes.

It was a man who had lost his way in the bogs. Bewildered with fear, he struggled towards the flickering light that seemed to promise help and safety. When the poor Moon saw him coming nearer and nearer to the deep hole, farther and farther from the path, she grew so angry and so distressed that she struggled and fought and pulled harder than ever. She could not get free, but she twisted and turned until her black hood fell back from her shining yellow hair. Its beautiful light drove the darkness away.

Oh, how the man cried for joy to see the light again! At once all the evil things fled into dark corners, for they cannot bear the light. Now he could see where he was, where the path lay, and how to escape the marsh. He was in such a hurry to get away from the quicksands, Goblins and Things that lived there that he barely looked at the brave light from the beautiful shining yellow hair. It streamed over the black cloak and fell onto the water at his feet. The Moon herself was so busy saving him, and so glad to see him back on the right path, that she completely forgot she needed help too, held fast by the Black Snag.

Off he went, exhausted and gasping, stumbling and sobbing for joy, running for his life out of the terrible bogs. Then the Moon realised how much she wanted to go with him. She pulled and fought as if she were mad, until she fell to her knees at the foot of the stump, worn out with struggling. As she lay there gasping for breath, her black hood slipped forward over her head. The blessed light went out, and the darkness returned, bringing all its Evil Things with a screech and a howl. They crowded around her, mocking, grabbing and beating her, shrieking with rage and spite, swearing and snarling. They recognised their old enemy, who drove them back into corners and kept them from carrying out their wicked wishes.
“Curse you!” yelled the witch-creatures. “You’ve spoiled our spells this whole past year!”
“And sent us to sulk in corners!” the Goblins howled.
All the Things joined in with a great “Ho, ho!” until the very grass tufts shook and the water gurgled. Then they began again.
“We’ll poison her—poison her!” the witches shrieked.
“Ho, ho!” the Things howled again.
“We’ll smother her—smother her!” whispered the Crawling Horrors, winding themselves around her knees.
“Ho, ho!” the rest mocked.
Again they all shouted with spite and malice. The poor Moon crouched down and wished she were dead and it was all over.

They fought and quarrelled over what to do with her until pale grey light began to appear in the sky and dawn drew near. Seeing this, they grew afraid that they would not have time to do as they wished. They seized her with horrible bony fingers and laid her deep in the water at the foot of the stump. The Goblins fetched a strange, great stone and rolled it over her to keep her from rising. They told two Will-o’-the-Wisps to take turns watching from the black stump, making sure she lay safely trapped and still, unable to escape and spoil their fun.
There lay the poor Moon, dead and buried in the bog until someone set her free. But who would know where to look for her?

Well, the days passed, and it was time for the new moon to appear. People put pennies in their pockets and straws in their caps to be ready for her, and looked about. The Moon was a good friend to the marsh folk. They were always very glad when the dark time ended, the paths became safe again, and the blessed Light drove the Evil Things back into the darkness and the water holes.

But days and days passed, and the new Moon never came. The nights stayed dark, and the Evil Things were worse than ever. Still the days went on, and the new Moon never came. Naturally, the poor people were terribly frightened and bewildered. Many went to the Wise Woman who lived in the old mill and asked whether she could find out where the Moon had gone.
“Well,” she said, after looking into the brewing pot, the mirror and the Book, “it’s very strange, but I can’t rightly tell you what has happened to her. If you hear anything, come and tell me.”

So they went away. As the days passed without a Moon, naturally they talked—my word, I should think they did talk! Their tongues wagged at home, at the inn and in the yard. Then one day, as they sat on the great bench in the inn, a man from the far end of the bog country sat smoking and listening. Suddenly he sat up and slapped his knee. “My goodness!” he said. “I’d completely forgotten, but I think I know where the Moon is!” He told them how he had lost his way in the bogs, and how, when he was almost dead with fright, the light had shone out. He had found the path and reached home safely.
They all hurried to the Wise Woman and told her. She looked for a long time into the pot and the Book again, then nodded.

“It’s still dark, children, dark!” she said. “I can’t see clearly. But do as I say, and you’ll find out for yourselves. All of you go, just before night falls. Put a stone in your mouth and take a hazel twig in your hand. Do not say a word until you are safely home again. Walk on without fear, far into the middle of the marsh, until you find a coffin, a candle and a cross. Then you will be close to your Moon. Look, and perhaps you will find her.”

So the next evening, as darkness fell, they went out together, each man with a stone in his mouth and a hazel twig in his hand. As you can imagine, they felt very frightened and uneasy. They stumbled and staggered along the paths into the middle of the bogs. They saw nothing, although they heard sighs and flutterings beside their ears and felt cold, wet fingers touching them. Then, as they looked for the coffin, candle and cross, they came near the pool beside the great stump where the Moon lay buried. Suddenly they stopped, trembling, bewildered and afraid. There was the great stone, half in the water and half out, looking exactly like a strange, huge coffin. At its head stood the black stump, stretching out its two arms like a dark, gruesome cross. On it a tiny light flickered like a dying candle. They all knelt in the mud and silently said “Our Lord”—first forwards because of the cross, then backwards to keep the Goblins away. They did not speak aloud, knowing the Evil Things would catch them if they disobeyed the Wise Woman.

Then they went closer, took hold of the great stone and pushed it up. Afterwards, they said that for one tiny moment they saw a strange, beautiful face looking happily up at them from the black water. But the Light came so quickly, so white and shining, that they stepped back in bewilderment. The very next moment, when they could see again, the full Moon was in the sky, as bright, beautiful and kind as ever. She shone and smiled down at them, making the bogs and paths as clear as day. Her light slipped into the very corners, as though she would have driven the darkness and the Goblins away altogether if she could.
